prize_parts.citation: For discoveries on the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which established the incretin principle underlying therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: I keep a single prize part on B025 and keep my trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, so my preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1. The scientific case is the same one the whole committee accepts: proglucagon processing, the incretin effect, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, satiety signalling and the identity of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide were worked out as physiology, confirmed over decades, and then validated by large independent outcome trials. Maturity is not in question. The chair asked whether the citation should be framed as physiology and the active peptide or as physiology plus therapy development. I answer physiology and the active peptide, because the question the prize answers is what was discovered about how the gut hormone works, and Drucker and Holst for the biology and Mojsov for the active form are all discovery-stage contributions. The clinical consequence is carried in the citation's final clause without making a drug designer a laureate. Having re-read the round-1 exchange, nothing has shown me that the discovery framing is wrong, only that the framing is a judgement and that the Knudsen trio is a coherent alternative.
statement.case_against: The weakness of my own configuration is that it leaves out Knudsen, whose acylated, albumin-binding analogues are the reason the discovery reached patients, and that it rests on Mojsov's priority for the active peptide, which is disputed by Habener's group and cannot be settled from the supplied material. Perlmann and Svenningsson are right that the half-life engineering was a mechanistic insight and not only a development exercise, and a prize that names the physiology but not the drug can be read as rewarding the story while omitting its engineer. If the committee concludes that the priority evidence for Mojsov is weaker than her credit suggests, my third seat becomes hard to defend and I would move to Knudsen rather than leave a contested name in place. A single-part prize also leaves out CAR-T and optogenetics, which have serious claims.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that the prize is for a discovery that reached patients, so Knudsen's long-acting analogues belong beside Drucker and Holst, and that a physiology-only prize would omit the step that made the discovery matter. He also says that if the committee wants physiology only, my trio would be the more defensible one.
responses.response: I accept the second part of his argument and not the first. The two framings do give different third seats, and I agree the choice follows from the framing and not from a difference in the quality of the science. I disagree that physiology omits the step that mattered, because the citation can state the therapeutic consequence without crediting its engineering. I also take seriously his point that the half-life work was a biochemical insight. What would move me to his trio is evidence, not framing: if the committee concludes that Mojsov's priority for the active peptide cannot be defended, the Knudsen trio is the better prize. I cannot make that call from the supplied material, so I keep Mojsov.

responses.point: The chair argues that a physiology-only prize makes Knudsen's seat hard to defend, while a drug-development reading makes the choice of academic physiologists hard to defend, so Drucker, Holst and Knudsen together span physiology, mechanism of action and the step that made the hormone usable.
responses.response: That is the strongest statement of the opposing case and I do not think the two failure modes are symmetric. A physiology citation is defensible on the Nobel tradition of rewarding discoveries, and it names the people whose work defined the mechanism. A combined citation carries the heavier burden, because it must justify leaving out both Mojsov and Habener while crediting industrial development, and the chair's own statement concedes that the credit problem is unresolved. On the chair's question about a second part, I keep my view that optogenetics is a discovery in physiology, since it has produced causal circuit findings, including in motor systems. Even so, I would not add it to a single-part prize while six names compete for three seats.

responses.point: Sandberg shares the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio but worries that a single-achievement prize leaves out CAR-T and optogenetics, which have serious claims, and she notes that Eshhar's priority is missing from the CAR-T credit.
responses.response: I agree about Eshhar and it is the reason I do not move CAR-T into a second part. A trio that we know to be incomplete is hard to defend, and the list does not let us repair it. On the broader worry I do not accept that a strong candidate left out of this year's prize is a reason to add a second part. A second part is justified only if its attribution can be defended as cleanly as the first. I keep CAR-T and optogenetics as alternatives, and I now name B047 as my second alternative in place of B051, because the committee exchange has shown wider support for CAR-T than for the unfolded protein response.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argues that the unanimous first place for B025 rests on substance and that the arc from the incretin effect through DPP-4 degradation to long-acting analogues is what makes delay hard to defend. She frames the prize as discovery plus development of long-acting agonists.
responses.response: I agree with her on the substance and on timeliness, and I do not think the committee should treat the GLP-1 question as anything but settled. I disagree only on where to draw the line for the third seat. The DPP-4 degradation insight that she credits to Drucker is already in my trio, so the biology of why native GLP-1 is short-lived is recognised without a development credit. I do not think that the delay point favours the Knudsen trio, since it applies equally to either configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the priority evidence for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide supports Mojsov over Habener, who is not among the credited names. This is the one fact that could change my third seat.
Whether the committee will frame the citation as physiology and the active peptide or as physiology plus drug development, which decides between Mojsov and Knudsen for the third seat.
Whether a second distinct achievement, B047 or B038, can be defended on clean attribution within the three-person limit, which I currently judge it cannot.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has arisen from the round-1 exchange. My field of motor-circuit neuroscience gives me context for optogenetics (B038), an alternative only, but I have no documented personal or institutional tie to any of its credited names. My documented 2009 co-authorship with Perlmann and my work with Grillner do not involve any shortlisted candidate or credited name, and I do not request a recusal.
